_about: Starter briefs given to researcher agents, written by the lead from general knowledge and explicitly marked 'may be wrong'. Records' `corrections` fields refer to these. Kept so corrections are checkable, and so the error rate of general-knowledge accounts can be measured.
monte-verde: Pre-Clovis occupation at ~14,500 years (Monte Verde II), excavated by Tom Dillehay; dismissed for about twenty years before acceptance; a 1997 site visit by skeptics is often credited with the shift. The older Monte Verde I claim (~33,000 years) is separate and still disputed. Expected status: vindicated.
white-sands: Human footprints dated ~21,000–23,000 years (Bennett et al. 2021, Science), initially dated with radiocarbon on Ruppia seeds; critics raised hard-water (reservoir) effects; later independent dating (conifer pollen radiocarbon and OSL, Pigati et al. 2023) is widely seen as settling the age. Expected status: vindicated.
jebel-irhoud: Hominin fossils found in the 1960s were long treated as Neanderthal-like and much younger; the 2017 papers (Hublin et al.; Richter et al., Nature) dated them to ~300,000 years (thermoluminescence on heated flints) and argued they are early Homo sapiens, pushing our species' origin back ~100,000 years and supporting a pan-African origin. Expected status: vindicated.
bluefish-caves: Excavated by Jacques Cinq-Mars from the late 1970s, who argued for occupation around 25,000 years ago; the claim was widely doubted for decades; in 2017 Bourgeon, Burke and Higham (PLoS ONE) re-examined the archived bone collections, identified cut marks and radiocarbon-dated them to ~24,000 cal BP. Expected status: vindicated.
piltdown: Announced 1912 by Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward as an early human ('Eoanthropus dawsoni') combining a large braincase with an ape-like jaw; exposed as a forgery in 1953 (Weiner, Oakley, Le Gros Clark), using fluorine testing among other evidence; a 2016 study (De Groote et al., Royal Society Open Science) argued a single hoaxer, most likely Dawson. Expected status: refuted (hoax).
calico-hills: Excavations from the 1960s directed by Ruth Simpson with Louis Leakey as a prominent backer, claiming stone tools tens of thousands (later ~200,000) years old; critics (e.g. C. Vance Haynes 1973, Science: 'artifacts or geofacts?') argued the flaked stones were produced naturally in alluvial fan deposits. Widely considered natural 'geofacts' today, though a few still defend it. Expected status: refuted (natural).
japanese-paleolithic-hoax: From the 1970s–1990s, amateur archaeologist Shinichi Fujimura 'found' stone tools at dozens of sites that pushed Japan's human history back to hundreds of thousands of years (claims up to ~600,000–700,000 years at sites such as Kamitakamori); exposed in November 2000 when the Mainichi Shimbun filmed him planting artifacts; the Japanese Archaeological Association's investigation later rejected his finds wholesale. Expected status: refuted (hoax).
cerutti-mastodon: A mastodon skeleton found during 1992–1993 highway construction; in 2017 Holen et al. (Nature) argued that broken bones and cobble 'hammerstones and anvils' show hominin activity ~130,000 years ago (uranium-series dating of the bones); strong critiques followed (e.g. in PaleoAmerica), arguing natural or construction-related breakage and questioning the dating. Expected status: open.
pedra-furada: Niède Guidon's team reported human occupation back to ~32,000 years (Guidon & Delibrias 1986, Nature) and later ~50,000; critics (Meltzer, Adovasio & Dillehay 1994, Antiquity) argued the 'hearths' could be natural fires and the 'tools' naturally fractured quartzite from rockfall. Later work at nearby sites reported further early dates. Expected status: open.
madjedbebe: Clarkson et al. 2017 (Nature) reported artifacts dating to ~65,000 years (OSL on single grains), implying earlier arrival in Sahul than the ~47,000–55,000 years many had accepted; an earlier 1990 TL/OSL claim of ~50,000–60,000 years at the same site (Roberts, Jones & Smith) also exists. Critics (e.g. O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS; Allen & O'Connell) argued artifacts may have moved down through sandy sediments (termites, trampling) and questioned the dating. Expected status: open.
denisovans: A new hominin group identified in 2010 from the mitochondrial genome of a finger bone (Krause et al., Nature) and then a nuclear genome (Reich et al., Nature), before any diagnostic skeleton; later fossils attributed via proteins or DNA (e.g. the Baishiya Karst Cave mandible, 2019; reportedly the Harbin cranium, 2025). Expected status: vindicated.
homo-floresiensis: Announced 2004 (Brown et al.; Morwood et al., Nature); critics argued the skeleton (LB1) was a pathological modern human (microcephaly, Laron syndrome, Down syndrome); the age was revised in 2016 (Sutikna et al., Nature) from ~18,000 to ~100,000–60,000 years for the skeletons; Mata Menge finds (2016, 2024) suggest small-bodied ancestors ~700,000 years ago. Expected status: vindicated.
paisley-caves: Gilbert et al. 2008 (Science) reported human mtDNA in coprolites dated ~14,300 cal BP; critics argued contamination (e.g. DNA leaching through sediments) and questioned whether the coprolites were human; Jenkins et al. 2012 (Science) added Western Stemmed points and further dating; later lipid-biomarker work (e.g. Shillito et al. 2020) addressed the human origin of the coprolites. Expected status: vindicated.
gobekli-tepe: Noted in a 1963 survey (Istanbul/Chicago) but not recognized; from the mid-1990s Klaus Schmidt identified Pre-Pottery Neolithic monumental enclosures (~9600–8200 BCE) built by hunter-gatherers before farming, framed as 'temples'; later debates concern the 'temple' interpretation (domestic or roofed buildings, e.g. Banning 2011), not the age. Expected status: vindicated or partial.
lanse-aux-meadows: The claim that Norse voyagers of the Vinland sagas reached North America; the site was identified in 1960 by Helge Ingstad and Anne Stine Ingstad and excavated through the 1960s; Kuitems et al. 2022 (Nature) dated wood cutting at the site to AD 1021 using a cosmic-ray radiocarbon event. Expected status: vindicated.
troy-hisarlik: The claim that Homer's Troy was a real city at Hisarlik (Frank Calvert in the 1860s; Heinrich Schliemann from 1870/71); the site is accepted as Troy/Wilusa, but whether a Trojan War like Homer's happened is still debated (e.g. the Korfmann–Kolb debate, c. 2001). Expected status: partial.
cardiff-giant: A carved gypsum figure 'discovered' in 1869, promoted as a petrified ancient giant or an ancient statue; commissioned by George Hull; exposed quickly (e.g. by Othniel C. Marsh, and Hull's own admission). Expected status: refuted (hoax).
glozel: Finds from 1924 by Émile Fradin, promoted by Antonin Morlet as Neolithic (or older) with an early alphabetic script; a 1927 international commission judged much of it fraudulent; 1970s thermoluminescence dates (e.g. McKerrell et al., Antiquity 1974) gave mixed ages; a later French ministry review (1990s) described a mix of periods plus possible forgeries. Expected status: refuted.
kensington-runestone: Found in 1898 by farmer Olof Ohman; its runic inscription is dated 1362; runologists and linguists judged it modern soon after (from 1899) and in later studies (e.g. Wahlgren 1958; Blegen 1968; recent work by Henrik Williams); proponents (Hjalmar Holand; later geological weathering claims by Scott Wolter) argue authenticity. Expected status: refuted.
bosnian-pyramids: From 2005 Semir Osmanagić claimed that Visočica hill and nearby hills are artificial pyramids tens of thousands of years old; geologists describe them as natural formations (flatirons); the European Association of Archaeologists issued a strongly worded statement in 2006; Science covered it (Bohannon 2006). Expected status: refuted (natural).
hueyatlaco: Excavated in the 1960s by Cynthia Irwin-Williams; stone tools with dates of ~250,000 years from uranium-series (Szabo, Malde & Irwin-Williams 1969) and tephra/geology (Steen-McIntyre, Fryxell & Malde 1981), far older than the excavator expected; the conflict between dates and artifacts was never resolved. Distinct from the Valsequillo 'footprints' in the Xalnene tuff. Expected status: open.
topper: Albert Goodyear reported pre-Clovis material (from the late 1990s) and in 2004 radiocarbon dates of ~50,000 years on charcoal from deep deposits; critics argue the deep 'artifacts' are natural chert fractures (geofacts) and the charcoal unassociated; geoarchaeological work (e.g. Waters et al. 2009) and later studies. Expected status: open.
meadowcroft: Excavated by James Adovasio from 1973; radiocarbon dates in the late 1970s implied occupation before ~16,000 radiocarbon years (deepest ~19,000); critics (e.g. Haynes 1980; Tankersley & Munson 1992) argued contamination of charcoal by ancient carbon (coal) and questioned the absence of Ice Age fauna; Adovasio et al. (1990) replied. Expected status: partial.
calixtlahuaca-head: A small terracotta head reportedly found in a sealed pre-Hispanic burial context by José García Payón in 1933; later identified by some as Roman (2nd–3rd century AD) style; thermoluminescence dating reported by Hristov & Genovés (1999, Ancient Mesoamerica) as pre-Columbian; critics (e.g. Michael E. Smith) question the find's provenance and documentation. Expected status: open.
sphinx-weathering: From 1991–92 geologist Robert Schoch (with John Anthony West) argued that the weathering of the Great Sphinx and its enclosure walls reflects prolonged rainfall, implying carving several thousand years before the conventional attribution to Khafre (~2500 BCE); critics (e.g. Harrell, Gauri, Lehner, Hawass) proposed salt weathering, flash floods, differing rock quality, and the archaeological context of the Khafre complex. Expected status: open (no decisive test has been run).
gunung-padang: Natawidjaja et al. 2023 (Archaeological Prospection) claimed Gunung Padang in West Java is a pyramid-like structure with construction phases back to ~27,000 years ago, from radiocarbon on soil samples and geophysics; the paper was retracted in 2024 after an investigation found no evidence the dated soils were associated with human construction. Expected status: refuted (as to ancient construction).
